name: Bianca Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a transmission crew, so the big steel towers, not the street poles. We work out of a depot in Red Hollow, about an hour from the city, and a normal day is a drive out to a right-of-way, a tailboard briefing, then hours in harness two hundred feet up replacing insulators or dampers on a 230-kilovolt line. Some days we're working off a helicopter platform, which still gives me a thrill after sixteen years. What wears me out is the drive and the waiting, for permits, for outages, for weather to clear.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who's waiting for you at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Lucas builds kitchens, and we have two girls, nine and twelve. We've got a mortgage on a place on Orchard Road and some savings tucked away, plus a small flat we rent out that my grandmother left me. I'm on our union's women-in-the-trades committee, because when I started there were two of us in the whole region. I use one of those AI chat tools now and then, mostly to tidy up incident reports so they don't come back covered in red pen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now can we talk about the stuff that actually matters, like staffing and heat rules. Nobody on my crew would care much. We'd joke that the chatbot still can't fix the depot coffee machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my life stays pretty much the same, and that's fine with me. I'd keep using the chat tool for reports because it saves me twenty minutes on a Friday. The towers will still need people for as long as I can see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing dramatic. Keep paying the mortgage, keep the rental going, keep working committee nights twice a month. Maybe push to get the depot a proper shade shelter, because last summer two of my guys nearly went down with heat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit flat, if anything, because so much noise ended up being about nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the noise was about nothing. Did any of it get to you before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. My older girl, Inês, came home asking if robots would take Mum's job because a YouTuber said so. I told her the robot would need to learn to pee in a bottle at two hundred feet first, and she laughed for ten minutes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's one thing you'd want to be different in ten years, even if AI changes nothing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More women on the towers, and better pay for the apprentices. When I started, I earned less than a cashier for two years, and a lot of good people quit because of that. That's nothing to do with computers and everything to do with who decides.

S0.say: Good, now we can talk about what matters on the towers, like staffing and heat rules. My crew wouldn't care much either way.
S0.think: My life stays about the same and I'm fine with that. I'd keep using the chat tool for reports because it saves me time, and the towers will still need people.
S0.do: Keeps her routine, mortgage, rental flat and committee nights going. Pushes the depot for a proper shade shelter after last summer's heat scares.
S0.feel: Calm, a bit flat after all the noise came to nothing.
S0.quote: I told her the robot would need to learn to pee in a bottle at two hundred feet first, and she laughed for ten minutes.
S0.fieldNote: Bianca is secure, practical and more concerned with conditions on the crew than with AI. Her daughter's question shows the fear reached her household even if it didn't reach her. She puts fairness questions, apprentice pay and women in the trade, ahead of technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change is fine as long as workers help shape it. If the company brings in drones for inspections or software for outage planning, the union should be in the room from day one. I'd post that on the committee group chat and probably at the regional meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think my job is fine, but the job around it changes. Drones already do some of our inspection patrols, and I've seen it go well and badly. The risk for me isn't losing work, it's ending up babysitting machines and losing the bit I love.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get on the first drone-pilot course the company offers, once a couple of other crews had tried it and said it was worth it. I'd push the union for a training fund paid by the company, not out of our dues. Money-wise, I'd keep saving as normal, I'm not worried about the bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. A little twinge about the helicopter days going away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about a time you saw the drones go badly.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We had a drone report a cracked insulator string as fine because the sun was behind it. A lineman named Dario walked out on it anyway because something felt off, and the bolt was half sheared. The drone saw a tower; Dario saw the tower he'd climbed in 2014.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait for others to try the course first. Why not go first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've been burned. They sent me on a 'new system' course in 2019 for software that was dropped eight months later. I'm happy to learn, I just want to know it'll stick around before I give up three Saturdays.

S1.say: Change is fine if workers shape it, and the union should be in the room from day one whenever drones or planning software come in. I'd say that at the regional meeting.
S1.think: My job's fine but the job around it changes. The risk isn't losing work, it's ending up babysitting machines and losing the climbing I love.
S1.do: Signs up for the company's drone-pilot course once other crews confirm it's worth it. Pushes the union for a company-paid training fund and keeps saving as normal.
S1.feel: Mostly fine, with a twinge of loss at the thought of fewer helicopter days.
S1.quote: The drone saw a tower; Dario saw the tower he'd climbed in 2014.
S1.fieldNote: Bianca's 'steady' adaptability shows clearly: she'll learn, but only once something has been proven, after being burned by a dropped system in 2019. Her worry is about losing meaning in the work, not losing income. The Dario story says a lot about how she values experience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need strong public rules and a strong union, and right now we have neither in time. I'd be calling for an emergency law to stop companies firing people straight into the street. I'd say it loudly, at work and online, and I'd probably march.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd be one of the last to go, because towers in the hills are hard for robots and I'm senior. But 'last to go' still means going. And with two years, my girls would be eleven and fourteen, and I'd have no clue what to tell them to study.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first months I'd sit down with Lucas and work out how long our savings and the rental income cover the mortgage, and I'd put the next six months of overtime straight into savings. I'd sign up for any retraining the union could get, maybe robot maintenance, since someone has to fix the things. I'd also push the committee to make sure women aren't the first cut, because we were the last hired.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not panicked. We've got a cushion, and Lucas's work is local.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'last to go still means going.' What's the moment you picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A robot crew truck pulling into the Red Hollow yard and the manager asking me to show it the right-of-way to Tower 112. I'd be teaching my own replacement where the wasps nest every August.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the girls about their future?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them learn things that need trust, like nursing, teaching, building something with someone. I honestly don't know if that's right. I'd probably say it with more confidence than I feel, because that's what parents do.

S2.say: This is exactly why we need strong public rules and a strong union, and right now we have neither in time. I'd call for an emergency law and I'd probably march.
S2.think: I'd likely be among the last to go because hill towers are hard for robots and I'm senior, but last to go still means going. I'd have no idea what to tell my girls to study.
S2.do: Works out with her partner how long savings and rental income cover the mortgage, and banks six months of overtime. Signs up for union-backed retraining such as robot maintenance and pushes to protect women from being cut first.
S2.feel: Anxious, though not panicked, because the family has a cushion and her partner's work is local.
S2.quote: I'd be teaching my own replacement where the wasps nest every August.
S2.fieldNote: Bianca's strong cushion keeps her out of real panic even in the fastest scenario. Her mind goes straight to collective protection, and specifically to women hired last being let go first. The image of teaching a robot where the wasps nest was the most striking moment so far.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message as the fast one, but with a plan attached. Five years is enough to set up a proper transition fund paid by the companies making the money from this. I'd be pushing that at the union and writing to our representative.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years makes me feel like I can steer it. I'd be forty-eight, with maybe a decade of good climbing left anyway, so I'd look at what comes after the towers rather than hoping they last forever. The girls would be fourteen and seventeen, so I'd have time to think about university with them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do the drone and robotics courses once the first crews came back saying they were real, and I'd start using the AI tools a bit more for planning work, not just reports. Lucas and I would put the rental flat's income straight into the girls' study fund. I'd stay on the towers but put my hand up to help design how the robots get used.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but with a sense of grip. Like having a rope tied off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would 'help design how the robots get used' look like in practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Me in a room with engineers telling them that a robot can't be left alone on a tower in a lightning season, and them actually writing that down. I've done hazard reviews for years. I know where people die on towers, and that knowledge shouldn't vanish because a machine is cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you sell the flat at any point?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not unless we needed it. It was my grandmother's, and it's the safest thing we own. If AGI meant it couldn't be rented, maybe, but I'd rather keep it for one of the girls.

S3.say: Five years is enough to set up a proper transition fund paid by the companies making money from this. I'd push it in the union and write to our representative about it.
S3.think: Five years makes me feel I can steer this, and at forty-eight I'd have about a decade of climbing left anyway. I'd plan for life after the towers and help the girls with their studies.
S3.do: Takes the drone and robotics courses once other crews prove them, and uses AI tools for planning work. Puts the rental income into the girls' study fund and volunteers to help design how robots are used on the towers.
S3.feel: Uneasy but with a sense of grip, like a rope tied off.
S3.quote: I know where people die on towers, and that knowledge shouldn't vanish because a machine is cheaper.
S3.fieldNote: Time makes Bianca noticeably steadier; she sees five years as enough to steer rather than react. She wants her safety expertise built into how robots are used. The grandmother's flat is both financial security and family meaning, and she guards it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if we use it, and a crime if we waste it. Every company bringing in robots should be training its own people to run them. I'd keep saying it at the committee, and I'd want it in our contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is close to fine for me. I'd be fifty-three, my knees would be telling me to come down off the towers anyway, and with the flat and our savings we'd be okay. The people I'd worry about are the young apprentices I'm training now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working on the towers for most of it and take the robotics courses in year two or three, once they've settled. I'd move into training or safety oversight around fifty. I'd also keep saving and push the union to protect apprentices, maybe by guaranteeing their places in whatever new jobs appear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not in a way that keeps me up. More like worry for others than for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which apprentice comes to mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya, she's twenty-two and she's the best natural climber I've seen in years. She's just started paying off a car. In ten years I'll be done and Priya will be thirty-two, right in the middle, with nothing to show for being brilliant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a gift or a crime. Which do you think it would be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably somewhere in between. Some companies would do it properly and some would wait until the last minute, the way they do with safety. Honestly I'm not sure, I'd like to think the union makes the difference.

S4.say: Ten years is a gift if we use it and a crime if we waste it. Every company bringing in robots should be training its own people to run them, and I'd want that in our contract.
S4.think: Ten years is close to fine for me, because at fifty-three my knees would want me off the towers anyway. The people I'd worry about are the young apprentices I'm training now.
S4.do: Stays on the towers for most of the decade and takes robotics courses in year two or three once they've settled. Plans a move into training or safety oversight around fifty, keeps saving, and pushes the union to guarantee apprentices' places in new jobs.
S4.feel: Uneasy, but more worried for others than for herself.
S4.quote: In ten years I'll be done and Priya will be thirty-two, right in the middle, with nothing to show for being brilliant.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Bianca's concern shifts almost entirely to the next generation. Her own path looks manageable thanks to savings, the flat and the natural end of a climbing career. Her worry for Priya was the most emotional moment in this section.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, AGI by 2028. I'd be fine for money, but I'd watch people I trained lose everything in a year, and there'd be no time to build anything for them. What would help is a public transition fund paid by the companies, real retraining with wages while you learn, and a union at the table when they decide who goes first.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who gets let go first. In every cut I've seen, it's the newest people, and the newest people are the women and the younger guys from poorer towns. We fought twenty years to get women up those towers, and I'd hate a robot to be the thing that sends us all back down.

headlineQuote: We fought twenty years to get women up those towers, and I'd hate a robot to be the thing that sends us all back down.
portrait: Bianca Santos is a 43-year-old transmission crew lead working high-voltage towers out of a rural depot, with a kitchen-fitter partner, two daughters and a rental flat she inherited from her grandmother. She's warm, funny and practical, uses AI tools now and then for reports, and adopts new things once others have proven them. She stays calm in the slow scenarios and becomes anxious but steady when AGI arrives in two years, cushioned by savings and the flat. With more warning, she plans to move into training and safety oversight. Throughout, she puts her energy into protecting apprentices and women in the trade.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because people she trained would lose everything within a year with no time to build anything for them.
whatWouldHelp: A public transition fund paid by the companies, retraining with wages while people learn, and a union at the table when deciding who goes first.
